questions.stem: Which of these is an う-verb (group 1)?
questions.explanation: A verb that does not end in -eru or -iru is always an う-verb, so 「飲む」 is group 1. 「食べる」, 「見る」 and 「起きる」 end in -eru or -iru and are る-verbs.

questions.stem: Which verb ends in -eru but is an う-verb (group 1)?
questions.explanation: 「帰る」 looks like a る-verb but belongs to group 1, which is why its ます-form is 「帰ります」, not 「帰ます」. It has to be learnt as an exception.

questions.stem: Which verb ends in -iru but is an う-verb (group 1)?
questions.explanation: 「入る」 (はいる) is one of the exceptions, so its ます-form is 「入ります」. 「いる」 (to be) is a regular る-verb: 「います」.

questions.stem: Which of these is a る-verb (group 2)?
questions.explanation: 「起きる」 drops 「る」 to make 「起きます」. 「入る」, 「帰る」 and 「はしる」 all end in -iru or -eru but are う-verbs, the exceptions every student learns as a list.

questions.stem: Which two verbs are irregular (group 3)?
questions.explanation: Only 「する」 and 「来る」 are fully irregular. 「行く」 is an ordinary う-verb with one odd form (「行って」), and 「ある」 is an う-verb with an odd negative.

questions.stem: What is the dictionary form of 「飲みます」?
questions.explanation: For an う-verb, the 「み」 before 「ます」 changes to 「む」. 「飲みる」 treats it as a る-verb, which it is not.

questions.stem: What is the dictionary form of 「帰ります」?
questions.explanation: 「帰ります」 is an う-verb, so 「り」 becomes 「る」. 「帰りる」 is the mistake of adding 「る」 to the stem as if it were a る-verb.

questions.stem: What is the dictionary form of 「来ます」, written in hiragana?
questions.explanation: 「来る」 is irregular: 「きます」 in the ます-form but 「くる」 in the dictionary form. 「きる」 is a different verb altogether (to wear, or to cut).

questions.stem: What is the dictionary form of 「します」?
questions.explanation: 「する」 is irregular, and it is the most used verb in the language because it combines with nouns: 「べんきょうする」, 「りょこうする」.

questions.stem: What is the dictionary form of 「まちます」 (wait)?
questions.explanation: The 「ち」 before 「ます」 belongs to the た-row, so it becomes 「つ」 in the dictionary form, as in 「もちます」 → 「もつ」.

questions.stem: What is the dictionary form of 「買います」?
questions.explanation: The 「い」 before 「ます」 becomes 「う」: 「買う」. 「買いる」 treats the verb as a る-verb.

questions.stem: What is the ます-form of 「帰る」?
questions.explanation: 「帰る」 is an う-verb, so 「る」 changes to 「り」 before 「ます」. 「帰ます」 is what you get by treating it as a る-verb, and 「帰れます」 is a different form meaning 'can go home'.

questions.stem: What is the て-form of 「食べる」?
questions.explanation: For a る-verb, replace 「る」 with 「て」. Only う-verbs change sound before 「て」.

questions.stem: What is the て-form of 「飲む」?
questions.explanation: う-verbs ending in 「む」, 「ぶ」 or 「ぬ」 take 「んで」: 「飲んで」, 「あそんで」.

questions.stem: What is the て-form of 「書く」?
questions.explanation: う-verbs ending in 「く」 take 「いて」: 「書いて」, 「聞いて」. 「書きて」 adds 「て」 to the ます-stem, which only works for る-verbs.

questions.stem: What is the て-form of 「行く」?
questions.explanation: 「行く」 is the one 「く」 verb that breaks the 「いて」 rule: its て-form is 「行って」. 「行いて」 follows the rule for 「書く」, which is exactly the trap.

questions.stem: What is the て-form of 「話す」?
questions.explanation: う-verbs ending in 「す」 take 「して」: 「話して」, 「かして」.

questions.stem: What is the て-form of 「まつ」 (wait)?
questions.explanation: う-verbs ending in 「つ」, 「う」 or 「る」 take a small 「っ」 and 「て」: 「まって」, 「買って」, 「帰って」.

questions.stem: What is the て-form of 「およぐ」 (swim)?
questions.explanation: 「ぐ」 verbs are like 「く」 verbs but voiced: 「いで」 instead of 「いて」. 「およいて」 forgets the voicing.

questions.stem: What is the て-form of 「あそぶ」?
questions.explanation: 「ぶ」 is in the same group as 「む」 and 「ぬ」, all of which take 「んで」.

questions.stem: What is the て-form of 「帰る」?
questions.explanation: Two rules at once: 「帰る」 is an う-verb, and う-verbs ending in 「る」 take 「って」. Treating it as a る-verb gives 「帰て」.

questions.stem: What is the て-form of 「来る」, written in hiragana?
questions.explanation: 「来る」 is irregular. Its て-form uses the same 「き」 as 「きます」.

questions.stem: How do you say 'Please write your name.'?
options: 名前を書いてください。
名前を書きてください。
名前に書いてください。
questions.explanation: A request is the て-form plus 「ください」. 「書く」 becomes 「書いて」, and the thing written takes 「を」.

questions.stem: What does 「今、テレビを見ています。」 mean?
options: I want to watch TV now.
I'm going to watch TV now.
questions.explanation: 「〜ています」 describes an action in progress. 'Going to watch' would be just 「見ます」, and 'want to' would be 「見たいです」.

questions.stem: What does 「姉はとうきょうにすんでいます。」 mean?
options: My older sister is moving to Tokyo.
My older sister lived in Tokyo.
My older sister wants to live in Tokyo.
My older sister lives in Tokyo.
questions.explanation: With 「すむ」 (live), 「〜ています」 describes a continuing state, so 'lives'. The past 'lived' would be 「すんでいました」.

questions.stem: What does 「ここでしゃしんをとってもいいですか。」 mean?
options: Shall we take a photo here?
May I take a photo here?
Did you take a photo here?
questions.explanation: 「〜てもいいですか」 asks permission: 'is it all right if I …?'. 'Please take' would be 「とってください」 and 'shall we' 「とりましょうか」.

questions.stem: How do you say 'You must not eat in the classroom.'?
options: きょうしつで食べてください。
きょうしつに食べてはいけません。
きょうしつで食べてはいけません。
きょうしつで食べてもいいです。
questions.explanation: 「〜てはいけません」 forbids. Eating is an action, so the place takes 「で」, not 「に」. 「〜てもいいです」 gives permission, the opposite.

questions.stem: What does 「朝ごはんを食べて、学校に行きました。」 mean?
options: I ate breakfast and went to school.
I went to school and ate breakfast.
I'll eat breakfast and go to school.
questions.explanation: The て-form links actions in the order they happen, and the tense comes from the last verb, 「行きました」. So both actions are past, breakfast first.

questions.stem: What does 「しゅくだいをしてから、テレビを見ます。」 mean?
options: While doing my homework, I watch TV.
Because I did my homework, I watch TV.
After doing my homework, I watch TV.
Before doing my homework, I watch TV.
questions.explanation: 「〜てから」 is 'after doing'. 'Before' is 「〜る前に」 and 'while' is 「〜ながら」.

questions.stem: What does 「すしを食べてみたいです。」 mean?
options: I'd like to try eating sushi.
I'm eating sushi to try it.
I don't want to eat sushi.
questions.explanation: 「〜てみる」 is 'try doing (to see what it's like)', and 「たい」 adds 'want to'. 'I've tried' would be 「食べてみました」.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「まどを___ください。」 (please open the window)?
questions.explanation: 「あける」 is the verb for opening something, so the request uses 「あけて」. 「あく」 means the window opens by itself, so 「あいて」 cannot take 「を」.

questions.stem: What is the ない-form of 「飲む」?
questions.explanation: For an う-verb, change the final u-sound to an a-sound and add 「ない」: 「む」 → 「ま」. 「飲めない」 is a real word, but it means 'can't drink'.

questions.stem: What is the ない-form of 「食べる」?
questions.explanation: A る-verb simply replaces 「る」 with 「ない」. 「食べらない」 treats it as an う-verb.

questions.stem: What is the ない-form of 「買う」?
questions.explanation: Verbs ending in 「う」 take 「わ」, not 「あ」, before 「ない」: 「買わない」, 「会わない」, 「言わない」. 「買あない」 follows the vowel rule too literally.

questions.stem: What is the ない-form of 「ある」?
questions.explanation: 「ある」 is an う-verb with an irregular negative: just 「ない」. The polite negative is 「ありません」.

questions.stem: What is the ない-form of 「来る」, written in hiragana?
questions.explanation: 「来る」 changes its vowel in every form: 「くる」, 「きます」, 「こない」. 「きない」 copies the ます-form.

questions.stem: What is the ない-form of 「帰る」?
questions.explanation: Because 「帰る」 is an う-verb, 「る」 becomes 「ら」 before 「ない」. 「帰ない」 is the る-verb mistake, and 「帰れない」 means 'can't go home'.

questions.stem: How do you say 'Please don't take photos here.'?
options: ここでしゃしんをとらなくてください。
ここでしゃしんをとらないでください。
ここでしゃしんをとってください。
ここでしゃしんをとりないでください。
questions.explanation: A negative request is the ない-form plus 「でください」. 「とる」 is an う-verb, so it is 「とらない」, not 「とりない」.

questions.stem: What does 「毎日しゅくだいをしなければなりません。」 mean?
options: I must not do homework every day.
I have to do homework every day.
I don't have to do homework every day.
I don't do homework every day.
questions.explanation: 「〜なければなりません」 is a double negative, 'if I don't, it won't do', which means 'must'. 'Don't have to' is 「しなくてもいいです」.

questions.stem: What does 「土曜日は学校に行かなくてもいいです。」 mean?
options: I can't go to school on Saturday.
I don't have to go to school on Saturday.
I must go to school on Saturday.
I must not go to school on Saturday.
questions.explanation: 「〜なくてもいいです」 is 'it's fine even if I don't', so 'don't have to'. 'Must not' is 「行ってはいけません」.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「あしたは早く___なければなりません。」 (I have to get up early tomorrow)?
questions.explanation: 「〜なければ」 attaches where 「ない」 would go. 「起きる」 is a る-verb, so its ない-stem is 「起き」 and the whole form is 「起きなければなりません」.

questions.stem: What is the plain past of 「食べる」?
questions.explanation: The plain past is the て-form with 「て」 changed to 「た」: 「食べて」 → 「食べた」. 「食べました」 is the polite past.

questions.stem: What is the plain past of 「行く」?
questions.explanation: Because the た-form copies the て-form, 「行く」 keeps its exception: 「行って」 → 「行った」.

questions.stem: What is the plain form of 「行きませんでした」?
questions.explanation: The plain past negative turns the 「い」 of 「行かない」 into 「かった」, as an い-adjective does: 「行かなかった」. 「行かないでした」 mixes plain and polite.

questions.stem: A friend asks 「きのう、何した？」 Which reply matches their casual style?
questions.explanation: Between friends the plain past is natural: 「見た」. 「見ました」 is correct but polite, and 「見たです」 is not standard Japanese.

questions.stem: What does 「日本に行ったことがあります。」 mean?
options: I have never been to Japan.
I want to go to Japan.
questions.explanation: Plain past + 「ことがあります」 describes an experience: 'I have (at some time) been'. The negative 「ことがありません」 means 'have never'.

questions.stem: How do you say 'I have never eaten sushi.'?
options: すしを食べなかったことがあります。
すしを食べたことがいません。
すしを食べたことがありません。
すしを食べることがありません。
questions.explanation: Experience needs the past 「食べた」 before 「こと」. With the dictionary form, 「食べることがありません」 means 'I never get to eat sushi', a habit rather than an experience.

questions.stem: What does 「しゅうまつは本を読んだり、えいがを見たりします。」 mean?
options: At the weekend I read a book and then watched a film.
At the weekend I want to read books and watch films.
At the weekend I don't read books or watch films.
At the weekend I do things like reading and watching films.
questions.explanation: 「〜たり〜たりします」 gives a sample of activities: 'things like … and …'. It does not fix an order, and the tense comes from the final 「します」.

questions.stem: Which pair completes 「日曜日は買い物をし___、友だちと会っ___します。」?
questions.explanation: Both verbs take 「たり」, and the sentence ends with 「します」. Leaving off the second 「たり」 is the most common error with this pattern.

questions.stem: What is the polite past of 「高い」?
questions.explanation: An い-adjective carries its own tense: 「い」 becomes 「かった」, and 「です」 just adds politeness. 「高いでした」 is the classic English-speaker error.

questions.stem: What is the polite negative of 「高い」?
questions.explanation: An い-adjective drops 「い」 and adds 「くない」. 「じゃない」 belongs to nouns and な-adjectives.

questions.stem: What is the polite past of 「いい」?
questions.explanation: 「いい」 comes from an older form 「よい」, and every form except 「いい」 itself is built on 「よ」: 「よかった」, 「よくない」.

questions.stem: What is the polite negative of 「いい」?
questions.explanation: As with the past, the negative is built on 「よ」: 「よくない」. 「いくない」 follows the regular rule, which 「いい」 does not.

questions.stem: What is the polite past of 「しずか」 (quiet)?
questions.explanation: 「しずか」 is a な-adjective, so it behaves like a noun: 「しずかです」, 「しずかでした」. 「かった」 belongs only to い-adjectives.

questions.stem: What is the polite negative of 「きれい」?
questions.explanation: 「きれい」 ends in 「い」 but is a な-adjective, so it takes 「じゃない」. 「きれくない」 treats the 「い」 as an い-adjective ending.

questions.stem: What is the polite past negative of 「たのしい」?
options: たのしかったじゃないです
たのしくなかったです
たのしいじゃなかったです
questions.explanation: Make the negative 「たのしくない」, then treat its 「い」 like any い-adjective: 「たのしくなかった」, plus 「です」. 「たのしくないでした」 puts the past on 「です」.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「このレストランは___、おいしいです。」 (cheap and delicious)?
questions.explanation: To link an い-adjective to what follows, change 「い」 to 「くて」: 「安くて」. 「で」 is the linking form for nouns and な-adjectives.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「この町はしずか___、きれいです。」?
questions.explanation: A な-adjective links with 「で」: 「しずかで、きれいです」, 'quiet and pretty'. 「な」 is only used directly before a noun.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「天気が___、あたたかいです。」 (the weather is good and warm)?
questions.explanation: Like its past and negative, the linking form of 「いい」 is built on 「よ」: 「よくて」.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「ゆうめい___人」 (a famous person)?
questions.explanation: Before a noun, a な-adjective takes 「な」: 「ゆうめいな人」. 「の」 links two nouns, as in 「日本の人」.

questions.stem: Which of these is a な-adjective, even though it ends in 「い」?
questions.explanation: 「きれい」, 「きらい」 and 「ゆうめい」 end in 「い」 but are な-adjectives, so they say 「きれいな花」 and 「きれいじゃない」.

questions.stem: What does 「このペンは書きやすいです。」 mean?
options: This pen is easy to write with.
This pen is hard to write with.
I want to write with this pen.
questions.explanation: The ます-stem plus 「やすい」 means 'easy to …'. 「書きにくい」 would be 'hard to write with'.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「日本に___です。」 (I want to go to Japan)?
questions.explanation: 「たい」 attaches to the ます-stem: 「行きます」 → 「行きたい」. It then behaves like an い-adjective.

questions.stem: How do you say 'I don't want to go.'?
options: 行きたいじゃないです。
questions.explanation: Because 「たい」 is an い-adjective, its negative is 「たくない」. 「たいじゃない」 uses the noun negative.

questions.stem: How do you say 'I wanted to go.'?
questions.explanation: 「たい」 → 「たかった」, exactly like 「高い」 → 「高かった」. The past belongs on the adjective, not on 「です」.

questions.stem: What does 「いっしょにえいがを見ませんか。」 mean?
options: We didn't watch a film together.
Would you like to watch a film together?
Didn't you watch a film together?
questions.explanation: A negative question with 「ませんか」 is a polite invitation. It is softer than 「見ましょう」, which assumes the other person will agree.

questions.stem: Someone asks 「あした、テニスをしませんか。」 Which reply accepts?
options: いいえ、しませんでした。
いいえ、テニスじゃないです。
いいですね。しましょう。
questions.explanation: Accept an invitation with 「いいですね」 and a 「〜ましょう」 form. The other replies answer it as a question about the past or about what the sport is.

questions.stem: What does 「まどをあけましょうか。」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「〜ましょうか」 offers to do something: 'shall I …?'. 'Please open' is 「あけてください」.

questions.stem: How do you say 'Let's go!'?
questions.explanation: 「ましょう」 attaches to the ます-stem, the same part that takes 「ます」: 「行きます」 → 「行きましょう」.

questions.stem: What is the potential form (can do) of 「話す」?
questions.explanation: An う-verb changes its final u-sound to an e-sound and adds 「る」: 「す」 → 「せ」, giving 「話せる」. 「話させる」 is the causative, 'make someone speak'.

questions.stem: What is the potential form (can do) of 「食べる」?
questions.explanation: A る-verb replaces 「る」 with 「られる」. 「食べさせる」 is the causative, 'make or let someone eat'.

questions.stem: What is the potential form (can do) of 「する」?
questions.explanation: 「する」 uses a different verb altogether: 「できる」. So 'I can play tennis' is 「テニスができます」.

questions.stem: What does 「かんじが読めますか。」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「読めます」 is the potential of 「読む」: 「む」 → 「め」 plus 「ます」. 'Do you read' would be 「読みますか」.

questions.stem: What does 「ピアノをひくことができます。」 mean?
questions.explanation: Dictionary form + 「ことができます」 is another way to say 'can'. 'Have played' would be 「ひいたことがあります」.

questions.stem: When someone gives something to you, which giving verb do you use?
questions.explanation: 「くれる」 is giving towards the speaker or their family. 「あげる」 is giving away from the speaker, and 「もらう」 is receiving.

questions.stem: What does 「わたしは友だちに本をあげました。」 mean?
options: My friend gave me a book.
I received a book from my friend.
I lent my friend a book.
I gave my friend a book.
questions.explanation: 「あげる」 is giving away from yourself, and 「に」 marks who receives. 'Lent' would be 「かしました」.

questions.stem: What does 「姉がわたしにペンをくれました。」 mean?
options: I received a pen for my older sister.
My older sister bought a pen.
My older sister gave me a pen.
I gave my older sister a pen.
questions.explanation: 「くれる」 always moves towards the speaker, and the giver takes 「が」. The same event from your side is 「姉にペンをもらいました」.

questions.stem: What does 「わたしは先生にじしょをもらいました。」 mean?
options: I received a dictionary from my teacher.
I gave my teacher a dictionary.
My teacher received a dictionary from me.
I lent my teacher a dictionary.
questions.explanation: With 「もらう」 the receiver is the subject and 「に」 marks the giver, the opposite job from 「に」 with 「あげる」.

questions.stem: Which verb completes 「友だちがわたしにプレゼントを___。」 (my friend gave me a present)?
questions.explanation: Giving towards the speaker needs 「くれる」. 「あげました」 would only work if the present went from you to someone else.

questions.stem: Which verb completes 「わたしは弟にゲームを___。」 (I gave my younger brother a game)?
questions.explanation: The gift moves away from the speaker, so 「あげる」. 「くれる」 can never have 「わたし」 as the giver.

questions.stem: Which particle completes 「わたしは友だち___ケーキをもらいました。」?
questions.explanation: With 「もらう」, the person you receive from takes 「に」 (「から」 also works). 「を」 is already used for the cake.

questions.stem: What does 「これは母がつくったケーキです。」 mean?
options: This is a cake my mother likes.
My mother will make this cake.
This is a cake my mother made.
This is a cake I made for my mother.
questions.explanation: 「母がつくった」 sits in front of 「ケーキ」 and describes it: 'the cake that mother made'. Japanese puts the describing clause before the noun.

questions.stem: In Japanese, where does a describing clause (like 'that I bought') go?
options: At the end of the sentence
questions.explanation: Everything that describes a noun comes before it in Japanese, clauses included: 「きのう買った本」, 'the book (that) I bought yesterday'.

questions.stem: Which phrase means 'the person who is reading a book'?
questions.explanation: The clause 「本を読んでいる」 goes straight before 「人」 with nothing between. Adding 「の」 is a common error, and the other two are whole sentences.

questions.stem: What does 「きのう見たえいがはおもしろかったです。」 mean?
options: The film I'll watch tomorrow looks interesting.
I want to watch yesterday's film again.
The film I watched yesterday was interesting.
The film I watched yesterday wasn't interesting.
questions.explanation: 「きのう見た」 describes 「えいが」, and 「おもしろかった」 is the past of 「おもしろい」. 'Wasn't interesting' would be 「おもしろくなかった」.

questions.stem: Which phrase means 'the bag I bought in Japan'?
options: 日本で買ったのかばん
questions.explanation: A plain-past clause goes straight before the noun, with no 「の」. English order, noun first, gives 「かばん日本で買った」.

questions.stem: What does 「子どものとき、オーストラリアにすんでいました。」 mean?
options: Before I was born, my family lived in Australia.
When I was a child, I lived in Australia.
When I have children, I'll live in Australia.
questions.explanation: Noun + 「のとき」 is 'when (I was) …'. The past 「すんでいました」 places it in your own childhood.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「ひま___とき、本を読みます。」?
questions.explanation: 「とき」 is a noun, so a な-adjective takes 「な」 before it: 「ひまなとき」, 'when I'm free'. A noun takes 「の」: 「子どものとき」.

questions.stem: What does 「日本に行ったとき、すしを食べました。」 mean?
options: If I go to Japan, I'll eat sushi.
I went to Japan because I like sushi.
When I went to Japan, I ate sushi.
Before I go to Japan, I'll eat sushi.
questions.explanation: A plain verb + 「とき」 is 'when …'. 「行った」 and 「食べました」 are both past, so both events happened.

questions.stem: Which completes 「本を読む___好きです。」 (I like reading books)?
questions.explanation: A verb cannot be the object of 「好き」 by itself; 「の」 turns it into a noun ('reading'), and 「好き」 takes 「が」. So 「読むのが好き」.

questions.stem: Which counter is used for long, thin things such as pens and bottles?
questions.explanation: 「〜本」 counts long, thin objects: pens, bottles, umbrellas, trees. 「〜まい」 is for flat things and 「〜ひき」 for small animals.

questions.stem: Which counter is used for flat things such as paper, shirts and tickets?
questions.explanation: 「〜まい」 counts flat objects: 「かみが一まい」, 「きっぷを二まい」.

questions.stem: Which counter is used for small animals such as dogs and cats?
questions.explanation: 「〜ひき」 counts small animals and fish, and its sound changes: いっぴき, さんびき, ろっぴき.

questions.stem: Which counter completes 「シャツを二___買いました。」?
questions.explanation: A shirt is flat, so it is counted with 「まい」: 「二まい」.

questions.stem: How is 「一本」 read?
questions.explanation: Before 「本」, 「一」 shortens to 「いっ」 and 「ほん」 becomes 「ぽん」: いっぽん. The same happens with six, eight and ten.

questions.stem: How is 「三本」 read?
questions.explanation: After 「三」 the 「ほ」 is voiced to 「ぼ」: さんぼん. 「なん本」 (how many) follows the same rule: なんぼん.

questions.stem: How is 「六本」 read?
questions.explanation: 「六」 shortens to 「ろっ」 and 「ほん」 becomes 「ぽん」, exactly as with 「一本」.

questions.stem: Which reading is right for one small animal, counted with ひき?
questions.explanation: 「一」 shortens to 「いっ」 and 「ひき」 becomes 「ぴき」, the same change as 「いっぽん」.

questions.stem: How do you say 'There are three dogs.'?
questions.explanation: After 「三」, 「ひき」 becomes 「びき」, as 「ほん」 becomes 「ぼん」. Animals are alive, so the verb is 「います」, not 「あります」.

questions.stem: How is 「二人」 read?
questions.explanation: One and two people have special readings: 「一人」 ひとり and 「二人」 ふたり. From three it is regular: さんにん.

questions.stem: How is 「四人」 read?
questions.explanation: Four people is よにん, which has to be learnt: 「よん」 shortens to 「よ」 here. 「よんにん」 is the regular-looking mistake, and 「し」 is not used for four people.

questions.stem: How is 「二つ」 read?
questions.explanation: The general counter 「〜つ」 uses the native numbers: ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ. 「ふつか」 is the second day of the month.

questions.stem: How is 「九つ」 read?
questions.explanation: The 「〜つ」 counter runs ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ, よっつ, いつつ, むっつ, ななつ, やっつ, ここのつ, and then 「十」 is simply とお.

questions.stem: How do you say 'two apples, please' when ordering?
options: りんごが二つください。
りんごを二つをください。
りんごに二つください。
りんごを二つください。
questions.explanation: A number with its counter usually comes after the noun and its particle, straight before the verb: 「りんごを二つ」. The thing asked for with 「ください」 takes 「を」, never 「が」.

questions.stem: How is 「三百円」 read?
questions.explanation: After 「三」, 「ひゃく」 is voiced to 「びゃく」. The same happens with 「何百」: なんびゃく.

questions.stem: How is 「六百」 read?
questions.explanation: 「六」 shortens to 「ろっ」 and 「ひゃく」 becomes 「ぴゃく」. 「八百」 does the same: はっぴゃく.

questions.stem: How is 「三千」 read?
questions.explanation: After 「三」, 「せん」 is voiced to 「ぜん」, just as 「ひゃく」 becomes 「びゃく」.

questions.stem: How is 「八千」 read?
questions.explanation: 「八」 shortens to 「はっ」 before 「せん」: はっせん. The 「せ」 stays unvoiced.

questions.stem: How is 「一万円」 read?
questions.explanation: 「百」 and 「千」 can stand alone for one hundred and one thousand, but 「万」 always needs 「一」: いちまん.

questions.stem: How do you write 10,000 in kanji?
questions.explanation: Japanese counts in groups of four digits, so 10,000 has its own unit, 「万」. 'Ten thousand' in English tempts you to write 「十千」.

questions.stem: How do you write 25,000 in kanji?
questions.explanation: 25,000 is two 「万」 and five 「千」: 「二万五千」. 「二十五千」 follows English 'twenty-five thousand'.

questions.stem: How do you write 120,000 in kanji?
questions.explanation: 120,000 is twelve 「万」, so 「十二万」. 「一万二千」 is 12,000 and 「百二十万」 is 1,200,000.

questions.stem: How is 「三分」 (three minutes) read?
questions.explanation: 「分」 is ふん after some numbers and ぷん after others. After 「三」 it is ぷん: さんぷん.

questions.stem: How is 「五分」 (five minutes) read?
questions.explanation: Two, five, seven and nine keep ふん: にふん, ごふん. The ぷん group is one, three, four, six, eight and ten.

questions.stem: How is 「六分」 (six minutes) read?
questions.explanation: 「六」 shortens to 「ろっ」 and 「ふん」 becomes 「ぷん」, as with 「ろっぽん」 and 「ろっぴゃく」.
